Abstract of Principles
ab'strakt əv prin'sə-pəlz
n. (the twenty-article confession of faith written by Basil Manly Jr. in 1858 for the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary)
Latin abstractus, drawn off, a summary; principium, a beginning, foundation.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Abstract of Principles is the confession of faith of the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary, drafted by Basil Manly Jr. at the request of the founders and adopted in 1858. It consists of twenty short articles drawn largely from the Second London Confession as it had been received in the Philadelphia and Charleston associations: on the Scriptures, God, the Trinity, providence, election, the fall of man, the Mediator, regeneration, repentance, faith, justification, sanctification, perseverance of the saints, the church, baptism, the Lord's Supper, the Lord's Day, liberty of conscience, the resurrection, and the judgment. Its doctrine of grace is plainly Calvinistic: election is God's eternal choice of some persons unto everlasting life, not because of foreseen merit in them; regeneration is a change of heart wrought by the Holy Spirit; and those whom God has accepted in the Beloved shall never totally nor finally fall away. Boyce insisted that every professor sign it, promising to teach in accordance with and not contrary to it, and that any departure be grounds for resignation. The seminary drifted from it in the twentieth century while still requiring the signature, and recovered it after 1993. Its purpose was Paul's: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a principle as a fundamental truth, a tenet, and an abstract as a summary containing the substance.

expand to see more

PRIN'CIPLE, n. Ground; foundation; that which supports an assertion, an action, or a series of actions or of reasoning; a tenet, that which is believed.

AB'STRACT, n. A summary or epitome, containing the substance, a general view, or the principal heads of a treatise or writing.

ARTICLE, n. A point of faith; a doctrinal point or proposition in theology.

Key Scripture

2Ti 1:13 — "Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus."

Eph 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:"

1Ti 6:3 — "If any man teach otherwise, and consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness;"

Jude 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Modern Corruption

Southern Seminary's Calvinistic confession, signed for a century by men who no longer held it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Abstract's history is a parable of confessional subscription. For much of the twentieth century professors signed a confession of unconditional election and the perseverance of the saints while teaching that Scripture erred and that election was a matter of human choice. A signature that binds no one has become what Paul warned against, consenting in form while one “consent not to wholesome words” (1Ti 6:3).

The principle to recover is the one the Abstract's recovery after 1993 demonstrated: a confession can be restored when trustees insist that it means what it says. Its article on election stands on Eph 1:4, “he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4), and it was written to be believed.

Usage

"“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — why the founders wrote it."

"“he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4) — the article on election."

"“consent not to wholesome words” (1Ti 6:3) — the drift of the twentieth century."
